newsitem.title: USA: Court review scuttles San Diego, Calif., bond plan.
newsitem.headline: Court review scuttles San Diego, Calif., bond plan.

text.p: The California state Supreme Court's decision to review San Diego's $200 million convention center financing has scuttled the city's plans to issue the bonds in the near term, officials said Friday.
A newly created San Diego financing authority had planned to come to market with the lease-revenue bonds in May to fund a one-million square-foot expansion of the city's convention center.
But those plans are now on hold, San Diego City Manager Jack McGrory said.
City officials said the San Diego bond deal was poised to proceed in May. Two state courts had already ruled that the financing was legal.
But this week, to the surprise of city officials and the bond professionals involved in the deal, the state Supreme court told San Diego that it would review the financing.

Even though the Supreme Court has only agreed to take on the case, municipal analysts warned that the court's mere involvement could hold up lease-revenue bond issues by other local governments in the state.

"It certainly raises some concerns that the court wants to consider a case about the appropriateness of lease financing," said Moody's Investors Service Inc vice president Ken Kurtz. "It's very surprising."

San Diego's attorneys said it could take the Supreme Court from 12 to 15 months to decide whether the issuance of the lease-revenue bonds through the San Diego Convention Center Expansion Financing Authority would be legal. The city maintains these revenue bonds do not require voter approval.
At least for the near-term, San Diego has put the $200 million bond deal "in the freezer," McGrory said.

"For now, we can't go to market with this joint powers authority and the lease-revenue bond structure we had in place," San Diego's city manager said. "We're going to have to look at other financing methods."
The city of San Diego has about $150 million of outstanding lease revenue bonds. Local governments in California have issued tens of billions of dollars of lease-revenue bonds over the last 10 years.
